valueChain.summary: Insurers collect premiums upfront, pay claims later, and earn money in two ways: the underwriting result (premium minus claims and expenses) and investment income on the float held between premium and claim. Distributors earn commission upfront without carrying risk, while reinsurers take a share of premium in exchange for absorbing large or concentrated losses.

stages.name: Product design and pricing
activities: Design cover, benefits and exclusions
Set premium rates from claims and expense assumptions
File products with IRDAI (use-and-file for most lines)
Write underwriting guidelines
revenueDrivers: Features customers pay extra for (riders, add-ons)

kpis.name: Expected loss ratio
kpis.benchmark: about 60-70% assumed in pricing for Indian retail health products (approx., varies by product and age band)

kpis.name: VNB margin (life)
kpis.formula: value of new business / annualised premium equivalent (APE)
kpis.benchmark: about 22-28% for large Indian private life insurers in FY25-26, after a 1.5-3.5 point hit from losing GST input tax credit; materially higher on pure term (approx.)

stages.marginNote: A small cost centre that sets the profitability of everything downstream: a 5-point pricing error flows straight into the combined ratio for years.

stages.name: Distribution and sales
activities: Generate leads and advise customers
Sell through agents, banks, brokers, dealers and online
Collect proposal forms and the first premium
players: Motor dealers (as motor insurance service providers)
revenueDrivers: Commission and rewards paid by insurers
Number and size of policies sold
costDrivers: Sales staff, agent recruitment and training

kpis.name: Commission ratio
kpis.benchmark: about 15% of gross premium for Indian general insurers overall in FY25; first-year life commission can reach 30-40% of first-year premium on some regular-premium products (approx.)

kpis.name: Active agent ratio
kpis.formula: agents selling at least one policy in the month / total agents
kpis.benchmark: no official industry figure; in Indian agency forces a minority of agents sell in any given month and sales are concentrated in a small top tier, so use the client's own trend and peer disclosures (illustrative)

stages.marginNote: Captures a large, low-risk share of premium: intermediaries are paid upfront and carry no claims risk, which is why insurers compete hard for bank and dealer access.

stages.name: Underwriting and issuance
activities: Assess risk (medicals, income proof, vehicle inspection)
Accept, load, decline or postpone proposals
KYC checks and policy issuance

kpis.name: Placement ratio
kpis.benchmark: roughly 65-80% for Indian retail term insurance, varying widely by channel (illustrative approximation)

kpis.name: Straight-through processing rate
kpis.formula: proposals issued without manual review / total proposals
kpis.benchmark: insurer-specific with no published industry benchmark; track the client's own trend by product and channel (illustrative)

stages.marginNote: A cost centre whose quality decides future claims: lax risk selection shows up one to three years later as a higher claims ratio.

stages.name: Policy servicing and renewals
activities: Collect renewal premiums (auto-debit, reminders)
Process endorsements, nominee and address changes
Handle complaints and grievances
Manage retention and portability requests
players: Insurers' operations teams and call centres

kpis.name: 13th-month persistency
kpis.formula: premium from policies still paying in month 13 / first-year premium of the same policies
kpis.benchmark: about 83-88% (premium basis) for leading Indian private life insurers in FY25; LIC about 75% (approx.)

kpis.name: Retail health renewal rate
kpis.formula: policies renewed / policies due for renewal
kpis.benchmark: commonly in the 80s per cent for established Indian retail health books (illustrative approximation; varies by insurer and age band)

stages.marginNote: Renewal premium is the most profitable premium because acquisition cost is low or nil, so persistency is a major value driver, especially in life.

stages.name: Claims management
activities: Register claim intimations
Survey, assess and authorise (cashless or reimbursement, in-house or via TPAs)
Check for fraud and settle
Recover salvage and third-party amounts
costDrivers: Claims handling costs (TPA fees, surveyor fees)

kpis.name: Incurred claims ratio
kpis.formula: net claims incurred / net earned premium
kpis.benchmark: India FY25, approx.: about 78% individual health, 92% group health, 95% government health; motor about 85% overall (about 75% at private insurers, above 100% at public sector insurers)

kpis.name: Claim settlement ratio (life)
kpis.formula: death claims paid / death claims decided, by count
kpis.benchmark: about 98-99% by count for large Indian life insurers (approx.)

stages.marginNote: The largest cost line: claims take roughly 80% of premium across Indian general insurance (industry incurred claims ratio about 83% in FY25), so a 2-point cut in leakage is often worth more than any expense programme.

stages.name: Investments, reinsurance and capital
activities: Invest the premium float and reserves
Buy reinsurance for large or concentrated risks
Hold solvency capital and match assets to liabilities
players: Reinsurers (the state-owned domestic reinsurer and foreign reinsurer branches)
revenueDrivers: Reinsurance commission received on ceded business

kpis.name: Solvency ratio
kpis.formula: available solvency margin / required solvency margin
kpis.benchmark: IRDAI control level 1.5; large private insurers typically report about 1.8-3.0 (approx.)

kpis.name: Investment yield
kpis.benchmark: about 7-8% on Indian insurers' largely government-bond portfolios (approx.)

stages.marginNote: Often where Indian general insurers actually make their money: investment income turns combined ratios of 100-110% into an overall profit.

valueChain.profitPools: In Indian general insurance most profit is earned on the float rather than on underwriting: industry combined ratios have tended to run above 100%, and investment income, especially on long-tail motor third-party reserves, covers the gap. Within underwriting, retail health and well-priced commercial property are the profitable pools, while group health and crop run near or above break-even. In life, protection (term) and non-participating products carry the highest new business margins, and distributors capture a large, low-risk slice through upfront commission, which is why exclusive bank partnerships are so valuable.

lines.item: Investment income on float (about ₹10,000 average float at 7.5%)

unitEconomics.result: Pre-tax profit per policy ≈ ₹1,500 (about 6% of premium)

valueChain.india: India is under-insured (total premiums were about 3.7% of GDP in 2024-25 against a global figure of about 7.3%) and tightly regulated by IRDAI, which sets product filing rules (now largely use-and-file), caps total expenses of management including commission and requires a solvency ratio of at least 1.5. Distribution is channel-led: banks dominate private life sales, dealers dominate new-vehicle motor cover, and aggregators and POSPs are growing fast. Motor third-party premiums are notified by the government rather than set by insurers; individual life and health policies have been exempt from GST since 22 September 2025 (group policies still attract 18%); and since February 2026 foreign investors may own up to 100% of an Indian insurer.

workedExample.problem: A retail health insurer's claims ratio rose from 62% to 70% in a year while premium grew 25%.
trace: Distribution (s2): most of the growth came from an aggregator partnership launched 18 months ago, but the commission ratio is flat, so acquisition cost is not the problem.

Claims (s5): cut claims by sales cohort. Policies sold in the last 18 months run at about 85%, while older cohorts are steady near 60%, so the deterioration is in new business, not in hospital costs across the book.
Underwriting (s3): to speed up online issuance, pre-policy medical checks were waived for applicants up to age 55 (previously 45), relying on self-declared health.
Product and pricing (s1): rates for the 45-55 band were set assuming medical screening, so the risk now accepted is underpriced.
workedExample.lesson: A claims spike is often caused upstream: cut claims by sales cohort and trace them back to how the risk was selected and priced.

cases.title: Motor insurer's underwriting loss widens
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Indian private general insurer whose motor portfolio earns about ₹3,000 crore of premium a year. Over two years its motor combined ratio has risen from 102% to 109%, turning an underwriting loss of about ₹60 crore into one of about ₹270 crore. Why has this happened, and what should the client do?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the combined ratio include? A: Claims incurred plus commission and operating expenses, divided by net earned premium. Investment income is reported separately.
Q: Has premium volume changed? A: Earned premium is flat at about ₹3,000 crore: policy count rose about 8% while the average premium fell.
Q: What is the mix of the book? A: About 55% own damage (OD), priced by the insurer, and 45% third party (TP), whose rates are notified by the government.
Q: What is the objective? A: Bring the combined ratio back to about 102% within 18 months without letting earned premium fall below ₹2,800 crore.

modelTree.label: Why has the motor combined ratio risen from 102% to 109%?

children.label: Number of policies by vehicle type (cars, two-wheelers, commercial)
Average premium per policy (OD discounts, TP tariff)
Average repair cost per claim (parts, labour)
Current-year third-party claims (number x award size)

hypotheses: Discounting on own damage to win dealer business cut the average OD premium about 10% while parts and labour costs rose, adding about 4 points to the claims ratio.
Third-party reserves for earlier years were strengthened after higher court awards, adding about 2 points that will not recur at the same level.
hints: The symptom is a ratio, so decompose the ratio itself before looking for causes.
Use four branches: earned premium, claims incurred, commission and acquisition costs, operating expenses.
Commission and acquisition costs split into channel mix (dealers, brokers, aggregators, agents) and the commission rate within each channel.

keyMetrics.name: Combined ratio
keyMetrics.formula: (claims incurred + commission + operating expenses) / net earned premium

keyMetrics.name: OD claims ratio
keyMetrics.formula: OD claim frequency x average OD claim cost / average OD premium

commonMistakes: Treating motor as one product: OD prices are set by the insurer while TP rates are notified, so the levers on each are completely different.
Ignoring prior-year reserve changes, which can move the ratio by several points without any change in this year's business.

frameworkPick.why: The client is asking why the margin of an existing business has worsened, so the answer is a profitability diagnosis across premium and every cost line.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: OD discounting is one suspect, but the deterioration could equally come from claims severity, reserves or commission, so starting with price narrows too early.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Claims handling may be part of the answer, but the symptom is a financial ratio that also moves with price, mix and reserves.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: A 109% combined ratio on one portfolio is not a capital or liquidity crisis; the insurer needs a margin diagnosis, not stabilise-and-restructure.

cases.title: Size India's pet insurance market
cases.prompt: A mid-sized Indian general insurer is considering adding pet insurance to its range. Before committing a team to it, the strategy head wants a quick estimate of how much pet insurance premium is written in India each year today. How would you estimate it?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Which pets? A: Dogs and cats only; there is no meaningful insurance offer for other pets.
Q: Which geography? A: All of India, but you can assume rural pet insurance is negligible.
Q: Today or in the future? A: Current annual gross written premium; a five-year view can come later.
Q: Any data to start from? A: Assume about 105 million urban households, of which roughly 10% own a dog or cat.

modelTree.label: Annual pet insurance premium in India today (urban dogs and cats)

children.label: Share meeting insurers' age and health rules (about 70%)
Share of insurable pets that are insured
Owners aware that pet insurance exists
Aware owners who buy a policy
Average annual premium per insured pet
Comprehensive plans (incl. OPD and third-party liability)

hypotheses: About 9.6 million urban dogs and cats are insurable, but only about 1% are insured, putting the premium pool at roughly ₹40-45 crore today.
Comprehensive plans are a minority of sales, so the average premium sits near ₹4,500 rather than the ₹8,000 headline price.
hints: Build a multiplication from a population down to premium, filtering at each step for who can and who does buy.
Three branches: number of insurable pets, share insured, average annual premium per insured pet.
Average premium per insured pet is a weighted mix of basic plans and comprehensive plans (share of buyers x premium for each).

keyMetrics.name: Premium pool
keyMetrics.formula: urban households x pet ownership x pets per household x eligible share x penetration x average premium

keyMetrics.name: Average premium
keyMetrics.formula: share basic x basic premium + share comprehensive x comprehensive premium

commonMistakes: Starting from India's total dog population, which includes tens of millions of community and street dogs that no one insures, and inflates the base many times over.
Borrowing penetration rates from mature markets such as the UK or Sweden, where a large share of pets are insured, when Indian penetration is around or below 1%.

frameworkPick.why: The question asks only how big the premium pool is today, which is an estimation built from population, penetration and price.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: Whether to enter comes later; the strategy head first wants the size of the pool.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: No product is being designed or launched yet; this is a sizing step before that decision.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Splitting pet owners into segments may help later, but the question asks for one total number.

cases.title: Double retail term insurance sales
cases.prompt: A private Indian life insurer writes about ₹600 crore of new retail term (pure protection) premium a year, 70% of it through its parent bank. The CEO wants to double this to ₹1,200 crore within three years. How should the client get there?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Why focus on term? A: Term plans earn roughly three times the margin of the insurer's savings products.
Q: What is the channel split today? A: Parent bank 70%, agency 15%, online aggregators and direct 10%, brokers 5%.
Q: Any constraints? A: No acquisitions, and medical underwriting cannot be relaxed because reinsurers carry most of the risk on term cover.
Q: How fast is the market growing? A: Retail protection premium in India is growing about 12-15% a year.

modelTree.label: How can retail term premium grow from ₹600 crore to ₹1,200 crore in three years?

children.label: Parent bank: customers approached x share who apply
Agency: active agents x term proposals per agent
Online and direct: visitors x share who apply
Medical tests and income checks completed
Underwriting decisions: accepted vs declined or postponed
Offers taken up by customers (incl. loaded premiums)
Premium rate per ₹1 lakh of cover (age, term, riders)

hypotheses: Only about 60% of bank-sourced term proposals become policies, mainly because customers drop out of medical tests; lifting this to 75% alone would add about ₹105 crore.
Agency term sales are small because agents earn more on savings products; aligning incentives could double agency term premium from about ₹90 crore to ₹180 crore.
hints: Treat new premium as the output of a sales funnel and break it into its multiplicative stages.
Three branches: more proposals logged, more proposals turned into policies, higher premium per policy.
Proposals logged split by channel: parent bank, agency, online and direct, brokers and new partners.

keyMetrics.name: Retail term new business premium
keyMetrics.formula: proposals logged x placement ratio x average premium per policy

keyMetrics.name: Placement ratio
keyMetrics.formula: policies issued / proposals logged

commonMistakes: Focusing only on lead generation and ignoring the 25-40% of term proposals lost in medicals and underwriting.
Proposing to loosen underwriting to issue more policies, which reinsurers will not accept and which would raise death claims later.

frameworkPick.why: The client wants to expand sales of an existing product through existing and new channels, which is a growth question about volume, conversion and ticket size.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The insurer already sells term in India; there is no new market to enter.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: Term is an existing product; the question is how to sell much more of it.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Margins are not the problem; term is already the most profitable line.

cases.title: Pricing an annual multi-trip travel policy
cases.prompt: A mid-sized German travel insurer sells single-trip policies for about €45 each. It has decided to add an annual multi-trip policy for frequent travellers within Europe. What price should it charge?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Who is the target customer? A: People taking three or more trips a year; they average four trips.
Q: What does cover cost? A: Expected claims are about €18 per trip for these travellers, and commission plus expenses take about 30% of premium.
Q: What do competitors charge? A: Two large rivals sell annual multi-trip cover at €119 and €139 with similar benefits.
Q: What is the objective? A: Win frequent travellers while keeping the product's combined ratio below 90%.

modelTree.label: What price should the annual multi-trip policy carry?

children.label: Cost floor: price needed for a combined ratio below 90%
Customer value: what frequent travellers will pay
Cost of buying single-trip cover for every trip (4 x €45)
Value of convenience and always-on cover
Rival annual prices (€119 and €139) and cover levels
Likely rival reaction to our price
Revenue lost from single-trip customers who switch
Revenue from new frequent travellers won

hypotheses: A price near €129 clears the €120 cost floor, sits inside the rivals' band and still saves a four-trip customer about €50 a year.
The main pricing risk is adverse selection: the most frequent travellers (eight or more trips) will buy first, pushing claims above €72 per policy.
hints: Bound the price from below and above, then test it against the market and against our own book.
Four branches: cost floor, customer value, competitor prices, net effect on our revenue.
Competitor prices split into rivals' current prices and cover levels, and how rivals are likely to react to our price.

keyMetrics.name: Minimum premium
keyMetrics.formula: expected claims per policy / (target combined ratio - expense ratio)

keyMetrics.name: Customer saving
keyMetrics.formula: trips per year x single-trip price - annual price

commonMistakes: Pricing off cost alone and landing at €120, leaving money on the table when customers would otherwise pay €180 for four single trips.
Forgetting that current customers who switch from four single-trip policies cut revenue per customer from about €180 to the annual price.

frameworkPick.why: The product decision is made; the only open question is the price point, set between a cost floor and the value to customers, checked against rivals.

distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The insurer has already decided to launch; the interviewer is asking for a price, not a launch plan.
distractorWhyNot.competitive-response: Rival prices are an input, but no competitor move triggered this decision.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: There is no existing profit problem to diagnose.

cases.title: Speeding up cashless hospital discharge
cases.prompt: A large Indian health insurer handles about 1.2 million cashless hospitalisation claims a year. IRDAI rules require final discharge authorisation within three hours of the hospital's request, but the client meets this on only 62% of claims and hospitals are complaining. The operations head blames a 10% vacancy rate among claims assessors. How would you get compliance above 95%?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Who processes the claims? A: In-house teams handle about 70%; the rest go through third-party administrators (TPAs).
Q: Where is the time going? A: The median is 2.5 hours, but 38% of requests take longer than three hours, and most of the slow ones involve a query back to the hospital.
Q: What does a delay cost? A: Under IRDAI rules the insurer bears any extra amount the hospital charges for delay beyond three hours, and complaints are reported to the regulator.
Q: Timeline and budget? A: Six months; the client is open to technology spend.

modelTree.label: How can three-hour discharge authorisation rise from 62% to 95%+ of 1.2 million claims?

children.label: Intake: request received to assessor assigned
Share arriving by email or scan needing manual entry
Assessor capacity by hour (evening discharge peak)
Routing rules (by hospital, by claim size)
Assessment: assessor picks up to decision
Time waiting on hospital responses to queries
Escalations for high-value or flagged claims
Integrated electronic channels (hospital portal, National Health Claims Exchange)

hypotheses: About 70% of breaches involve at least one query; a standard discharge document checklist agreed with the top 500 network hospitals would remove about half of them.
Breaches cluster between 5 pm and 10 pm, when discharges peak but assessor rosters are thin.
TPA-handled claims breach at about twice the in-house rate because of hand-off delays.
hints: Follow the clock: break the three hours into the sequential steps a request passes through.
Three stages: intake, assessment, communication of the decision.
Communication splits into integrated electronic channels (hospital portal, National Health Claims Exchange) and manual channels (email, phone).

keyMetrics.name: Three-hour compliance
keyMetrics.formula: discharge authorisations issued within 3 hours / total discharge requests

keyMetrics.name: Query rate
keyMetrics.formula: discharge requests with at least one query / total discharge requests

keyMetrics.name: Hourly capacity gap
keyMetrics.formula: requests arriving per hour x handling time - assessor hours available that hour

commonMistakes: Hiring assessors across the board when delays are concentrated in hospital queries and the evening peak.
Chasing speed alone: auto-approving bills without checks raises claims leakage, so controls must be redesigned rather than dropped.

frameworkPick.why: The client must cut the time taken by a defined process to meet a service standard, which calls for a process-step breakdown of where time is lost.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Delay penalties cost money, but the question is about process speed, not margin.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: The insurer is not in financial distress; one process is underperforming.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Splitting claims by hospital or channel helps the analysis, but the question is how to fix a process.

cases.title: European insurer weighs Indian health entry
cases.prompt: A mid-sized European health insurer is looking at India now that foreign investors may own up to 100% of an Indian insurer, a change in force since February 2026. Indian health insurance premiums are about ₹1.2 lakh crore a year and growing roughly 9-10% a year. Its CEO believes the client's highly rated digital claims app will be the main way to win customers. Should the client enter, and if so, how?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the client's ambition? A: About ₹5,000 crore of annual premium within ten years, with an underwriting break-even within seven.
Q: What are its strengths? A: Private medical insurance and hospital network management in three European markets; no presence in Asia.
Q: How much capital can it commit? A: Up to €300 million (roughly ₹3,000 crore).

Q: What routes are open? A: A new standalone health insurance licence, buying a controlling or full stake in an existing Indian insurer, or a joint venture with an Indian group. Foreign ownership up to 100% is under the automatic route, but the insurer still needs IRDAI registration and at least one of its chair, managing director or CEO must be a resident Indian citizen.

modelTree.label: Should the client enter Indian health insurance, and how, to reach ₹5,000 crore?

children.label: Claims ratios (individual about 70-80%, group and government about 90-95%)
Distribution costs and channel bargaining power
Product and claims rules (cashless timelines, portability)
Standalone health insurers' share and scale
Transferable strengths (hospital network management, medical underwriting)
Gaps to close (Indian distribution, low-cost operations)
Time to licence and to build distribution
Buy: controlling stake in an existing insurer
Quality of the acquired book and network
Partner: joint venture with an Indian group
Access to the partner's customers and channels
Do the economics meet the target?
Premium path to ₹5,000 crore (about 1.6% share in year ten)
Capital needed vs the €300 million budget

hypotheses: Retail health is the attractive pool (claims ratios of roughly 70-80% against 90-95% in group and government business), but it is distribution-led, so a greenfield entrant is unlikely to reach ₹5,000 crore in ten years without a bank or large agency partner.
Buying a controlling stake in a sub-scale standalone health insurer gives the client a licence, hospital network and agents immediately, and fits within €300 million.
hints: Separate 'should we' from 'how': judge the opportunity and the client's fit first, then the route and the numbers.
Four branches: is the market attractive, can the client win, which entry route, do the economics meet the target.
Can the client win splits into competitors (standalone health insurers, general insurers' health books), transferable strengths and gaps to close.

keyMetrics.name: Required market share
keyMetrics.formula: ₹5,000 crore / market in year ten (₹1.2 lakh crore x 1.1^10 ≈ ₹3.1 lakh crore, assuming 10% growth) ≈ 1.6%

keyMetrics.name: Combined ratio
keyMetrics.formula: claims ratio + commission ratio + operating expense ratio

commonMistakes: Treating the whole ₹1.2 lakh crore as addressable when group and government business is price-driven and runs near break-even.
Accepting the CEO's view that a claims app will win customers, when distribution (banks, agents, brokers) is the scarce asset in Indian insurance.

frameworkPick.why: A company with no presence in India must decide whether to enter and by which route, which is exactly what the entry framework covers: market, ability to win, mode and economics.

distractorWhyNot.ma: An acquisition is one of three routes to compare, not the question itself.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Growth frameworks assume an existing business to expand; the client has none in India.
distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Market size is one input to attractiveness; the question is whether and how to enter.

cases.title: Launching pay-as-you-drive car insurance
cases.prompt: A large Indian private general insurer wants to launch a telematics-based pay-as-you-drive add-on for private car own-damage cover, which IRDAI has permitted since 2022. Its data suggests about 20% of urban car owners drive under 5,000 km a year. About 60% of its private car book is sold and renewed through dealers. How should the client launch this product, and is it worth doing?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the client's current position? A: It insures about 2.5 million private cars at an average own-damage premium of about ₹9,000.
Q: What design is proposed? A: Own-damage discounts of 15-25% for low-mileage drivers, with kilometres recorded by a smartphone app or a plug-in device.
Q: What is the objective? A: Win low-risk drivers from rivals and improve the own-damage claims ratio, now about 72%.
Q: Timeline and scope? A: Launch within nine months in the top eight cities.

modelTree.label: How should the client launch pay-as-you-drive OD cover, and is it worth it?

children.label: Size of the low-mileage segment in the top eight cities
Car owners driving under 5,000 km a year (about 20%)
Share willing to share driving data
Value of the saving (about ₹1,350-2,250 a year)
Barriers: tracking effort and data privacy
Rules when drivers exceed their kilometre band
Dealers' and brokers' incentive to sell a lower premium
Premium given up on existing low-mileage customers who switch
New low-risk customers won from rivals

hypotheses: Low-mileage drivers already run an OD claims ratio near 55% against the 72% book average, so a 15-20% discount is affordable on new customers.
The main risk is cannibalisation: if most take-up comes from the client's own low-mileage customers, premium falls 15-25% on its most profitable cars with no fall in claims.
Dealers, who sell much of new-car OD cover, will resist because their commission falls with premium, so renewals and digital channels should lead.
hints: Ask the questions a launch committee would ask, in order, before signing off a budget.
Four branches: customer demand, product and pricing design, go-to-market, economics and risks.
Product and pricing design splits into the discount structure by kilometre band, the tracking method (accuracy, tampering, cost) and rules when drivers exceed their band.

keyMetrics.name: Net premium effect
keyMetrics.formula: new customers x discounted premium - switching existing customers x discount given

keyMetrics.name: Low-mileage claims ratio
keyMetrics.formula: OD claims of low-mileage cohort / OD earned premium of that cohort

commonMistakes: Assuming all take-up is new business, when switchers from the existing book can make the launch premium-negative.
Ignoring tampering and disputes over kilometres driven, which decide whether the discount can be defended at claim time.

frameworkPick.why: The client is introducing a new product to existing markets and must judge demand, design, channels and economics, which is the product launch structure.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Discount design is one part, but the question also covers demand, channels and whether the launch pays off.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The client already writes motor insurance in these cities.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Identifying low-mileage drivers matters, but the decision is about launching and selling the product.

cases.title: Prioritising e-wallet users for embedded cover
cases.prompt: A Southeast Asian digital insurer sells travel, phone-screen and hospital cash cover inside a large e-wallet app with 30 million monthly active users. Only 0.4% of users bought a policy last year, and its US$6 million marketing budget is spread evenly across the base. The e-wallet partner suggests targeting its highest spenders. How should the client segment users to decide where to focus?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Which markets? A: Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam, all through the same e-wallet partner.
Q: What data is available? A: With user consent: transaction categories (travel bookings, electronics, healthcare, bill payments), app usage, wallet spend and age band.
Q: What are the economics? A: Average annual premium is about US$35 per buyer; the e-wallet takes a 20% fee; marketing cost per buyer is about US$50.
Q: What is the objective? A: Double the number of buyers within a year without increasing the marketing budget.

modelTree.label: Which user segments should the US$6 million budget target to double buyers?

children.label: Dimensions to cut the base on
Past use of in-app financial products
Has used pay-later, savings or investments
Lift from offers timed to the trigger
Rank segments by margin per marketing dollar
Offer design and timing (e.g. at checkout)

hypotheses: Users who have just booked travel convert at 3-5% when offered cover at checkout against 0.4% on average, so trigger-timed offers alone could double buyers on the same budget.
Electronics buyers are the largest trigger group, but phone-screen cover has a high claims ratio (about 60%), so they rank lower on margin per marketing dollar than their size suggests.
hints: A segmentation answer is a sequence of decisions, not a list of segments: structure the steps.
Three branches: dimensions to cut the base on, attractiveness of each segment, targeting the chosen segments.
Targeting the chosen segments splits into how you rank them and how you design and time the offer.

keyMetrics.name: Margin per marketing dollar
keyMetrics.formula: conversion x (premium - claims - wallet fee - servicing) / marketing cost per targeted user

keyMetrics.name: Conversion rate
keyMetrics.formula: buyers / users targeted

commonMistakes: Following the partner's advice to target high spenders, or segmenting on age and income; in embedded insurance the purchase trigger (a trip, a phone purchase) predicts buying far better.
Ranking segments by number of buyers rather than by margin after claims and the wallet's 20% fee.

frameworkPick.why: The client has a fixed budget and a large undifferentiated user base, and must split users into groups and rank them, which is a segmentation and targeting problem.

distractorWhyNot.growth: The goal is more buyers, but the question asks specifically how to split users and allocate a fixed budget.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Price is not raised as an issue; conversion and targeting are.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: All three products already exist in the app.

cases.title: Responding to a cheaper health rival
cases.prompt: Our client is a leading Indian standalone health insurer with ₹8,000 crore of retail premium. A newly licensed insurer backed by a large consumer-internet group has launched an online-only family floater priced about 15% below the client's, with a 30-day waiting period for pre-existing diseases. It is backing the launch with a television campaign fronted by a well-known cricketer. Online sales are 12% of the client's retail new business. How should the client respond?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What has the impact been so far? A: In three months the client's online new business is down 18%; renewals have not yet been affected.
Q: How does the client's product compare? A: It has a three-year waiting period for pre-existing diseases, and the retail book runs at a claims ratio of about 62%.

Q: What do we know about the entrant? A: Its parent can fund losses for several years; the plan is sold only on its own app and two aggregators. The 30-day pre-existing disease wait is the entrant's own design choice: Indian retail plans typically use one to three years, and IRDAI caps the wait at three years.
Q: What is the objective? A: Keep retail premium growing about 15% a year without letting the retail claims ratio exceed 65%.

modelTree.label: How should the client respond to the entrant's cheaper, short-waiting-period floater?

children.label: Likely claims ratio with a 30-day pre-existing disease wait
Assess the impact on the client
Online and aggregators (12% of new business)
Effect on the claims ratio of those who stay
Match on price or waiting period
Online-only variant with shorter wait and loading
Differentiate on proposition (hospital network, claims service)
Strengthen channels the entrant cannot reach (agency, bancassurance)
Effect on retail growth against the 15% target
Effect on the claims ratio against the 65% ceiling

hypotheses: The threat is concentrated online, about 12% of new business, so a book-wide price cut would give away margin on the 88% the entrant cannot reach.
A 30-day pre-existing disease wait will attract sicker customers, so the entrant's claims ratio is likely to exceed 85% within two years, making the price hard to sustain.
The bigger long-term risk is renewals: healthy younger policyholders porting out would push the client's claims ratio up.
hints: Work in sequence from the rival's move through to your decision.
Four branches: understand the entrant's move, assess the impact on the client, response options, choose the response.
Understanding the entrant's move splits into whether the offer is sustainable (its likely claims ratio, the parent's funding) and whom it targets (segments, channels).

keyMetrics.name: Retail claims ratio
keyMetrics.formula: retail claims incurred / retail earned premium

keyMetrics.name: Premium at risk
keyMetrics.formula: online new business x share lost + renewal premium of likely porters

commonMistakes: Matching the price across the whole book instead of ring-fencing the response to the online segment.
Ignoring adverse selection: copying a 30-day waiting period can raise claims far more than the premium it protects.

frameworkPick.why: A specific rival move has hit sales, and the client needs to judge the threat, size the damage and choose among responses, which is the competitive response structure.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Price is one response option, but the question is broader: whether to respond at all, where and how.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Profits have not yet fallen; the issue is a competitive threat to growth.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: It is the rival that is entering; the client is already established.

cases.title: Turning around a state-owned general insurer
cases.prompt: A state-owned Indian general insurer writes about ₹18,000 crore of gross premium but runs a combined ratio of about 122%, and its solvency ratio has fallen to 1.1 against IRDAI's minimum of 1.5. The government has said there will be no more capital and wants the insurer to keep participating in crop and government health schemes. What should management do over the next 24 months?
clarifyingFacts: Q: How does each line perform? A: Group health is 30% of premium at a combined ratio of about 140%; motor 30% at 125%; fire and engineering 20% at 98%; crop and government schemes 15% at 112%; other lines 5% at 115%.
Q: How do expenses compare? A: Operating expenses are about 18% of premium against 12-13% at large private peers, mainly staff costs across about 1,800 offices.
Q: What about investments? A: An investment book of about ₹35,000 crore yields about 7.5% and carries large unrealised gains on equities.
Q: Any constraints? A: No compulsory layoffs, though voluntary retirement is possible; scheme participation must continue, but its terms can be renegotiated.

modelTree.label: How can solvency rise from 1.1 to 1.5+ in 24 months without government capital?

children.label: Premium adequacy: reprice group health and motor OD, renegotiate scheme rates
Claims cost: hospital tariffs, fraud and leakage controls
Expenses: voluntary retirement, merge offices (18% vs peers' 12-13%)
Improve the investment result on ₹35,000 crore
Realise equity gains (check solvency treatment of unrealised gains)
Rebalance for yield within liquidity needs
Raise capital from sources other than the government
Subordinated debt and other permitted forms of capital
Minority stake sale or stock market listing
Quota-share treaties on motor and health
Cost of ceding vs capital relief gained
Change the volume and mix of business written
Cap volume in capital-heavy, loss-making lines

hypotheses: Group health (30% of premium at about 140%) drives over half of the underwriting loss, so repricing or exiting the worst corporate accounts is the single biggest lever.
Crop and government schemes cause only about 8% of the underwriting loss, so the government's demand to keep them is compatible with the turnaround if rates are renegotiated.
Reinsurance and subordinated debt can close most of the solvency gap within 12 months, buying time for slower fixes such as voluntary retirement.
hints: The target is a ratio with a deadline: attack both sides of it.
Two branches: raise available solvency margin (underwriting result, investment result, outside capital) and lower required solvency margin (reinsurance, volume and mix).
Lower required solvency margin splits into ceding more risk through reinsurance (capital relief vs cost) and changing the volume and mix of business written.

keyMetrics.name: Solvency ratio
keyMetrics.formula: available solvency margin / required solvency margin (IRDAI minimum 1.5)

keyMetrics.name: Loss contribution by line
keyMetrics.formula: line share of premium x (line combined ratio - 100%)

keyMetrics.name: Combined ratio
keyMetrics.formula: (net claims incurred + commission + operating expenses) / net earned premium

commonMistakes: Blaming government schemes for the losses without checking the numbers: at about 8% of the underwriting loss they matter far less than group health and motor.
Treating it as a pure profit problem; repricing takes two to three years to flow through, so capital-side levers (reinsurance, subordinated debt) are needed to hit the 24-month solvency target.

frameworkPick.why: The insurer faces a capital crisis with a hard deadline and no outside equity, which calls for a turnaround (stabilise capital first, then fix the core); the core fix is a profitability diagnosis by line and cost item.

distractorWhyNot.operations: Claims and expense processes matter, but they sit inside the profitability fix and do nothing for capital on their own.
distractorWhyNot.ma: A merger with another state insurer might be a long-term option, but the 24-month solvency gap has to be closed by the insurer itself.

cases.title: Buying a UK motor insurer post-reform
cases.prompt: A large continental European insurer is considering buying a UK motor insurer with £1.4 billion of gross written premium for about £900 million. The target's management points to a five-year average combined ratio of 94% and customer retention of about 80% as proof of a strong franchise. Should the client buy it, and at what price?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the year-by-year record? A: Combined ratio was 86% in 2021, 91% in 2022, 98% in 2023, 99% in 2024 and 96% in 2025.

Q: What changed in the market? A: Since 1 January 2022 the FCA's general insurance pricing rules have banned quoting renewing home and motor customers more than an equivalent new customer through the same channel; before that, the target's renewing customers paid on average about 15% more (a case assumption).
Q: What is the client's rationale? A: It writes only about £300 million of UK motor premium and wants scale in claims purchasing, pricing data and IT.
Q: Other financials? A: Investment income is about £40 million a year; UK corporation tax is 25%.

modelTree.label: Should the client buy the UK motor insurer for about £900 million, and at what price?

children.label: Value of scale (from £300 million to £1.7 billion of premium)
Claims purchasing power (repairers, parts, hire cars)
Underwriting result after the 2022 pricing rules
Renewal margin lost on loyal customers
Claims inflation (repair costs, used car values)
Investment income on the float (about £40 million)
Prior-year reserve releases in reported results
Bodily injury reserves (Ogden discount rate, +0.5% since January 2025)
At 94% combined: about £93 million net, about 10x
At an underlying 98%: about £51 million net, about 18x
FCA fair value reviews of add-ons

hypotheses: The 94% average flatters the target: 2021-22 results included renewal margins now banned, so the sustainable combined ratio is nearer 98%, cutting pre-tax earnings by almost half.
High retention no longer signals pricing power; since 2022 it reflects fair renewal pricing, so it should not earn a premium in the valuation.
Claims supply-chain synergies of 2-3 points on the combined £1.7 billion book (about £34-51 million a year pre-tax) are the only route to justifying a price near £900 million.
hints: Use the standard acquisition structure, but weight it towards the one question that decides the price.
Four branches: strategic fit, sustainable standalone earnings, net synergies, price and deal risks.
Net synergies split into cost synergies (IT platform, claims operations and supply chain), revenue synergies and integration costs.

keyMetrics.name: Sustainable net earnings
keyMetrics.formula: (GWP x (1 - combined ratio) + investment income) x (1 - 25% tax)

keyMetrics.name: Implied P/E
keyMetrics.formula: purchase price / sustainable net earnings

keyMetrics.name: Synergy value
keyMetrics.formula: run-rate synergies x (1 - tax) x multiple - one-off integration costs

commonMistakes: Taking the five-year average combined ratio at face value when a regulatory change in 2022 broke the series.
Paying for revenue synergies such as cross-selling home cover, which are hard to deliver in a market where most customers buy through price comparison sites.

frameworkPick.why: It is an acquisition decision (fit, standalone value, synergies, price), but the crux is a profitability question: what the target earns once the banned renewal margin is stripped out.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The client already writes UK motor insurance, so this is about scale, not entry.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: The buyer is a strategic insurer seeking synergies, not a financial investor planning an exit.

cases.title: PE stake in an SME insurance broker
cases.prompt: A private equity fund is considering buying 60% of an Indian insurance broker that places group health and property cover for about 9,000 small and mid-sized businesses, at a valuation of ₹2,000 crore for the whole company. Revenue has grown 35% a year to ₹320 crore at a 25% EBITDA margin, and management projects 30% annual growth for five more years. Should the fund invest?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What makes up revenue? A: About 60% is base brokerage and 40% is rewards and marketing fees paid by insurers; three insurers account for 55% of revenue. The rewards need almost no extra staff or servicing, so nearly all of that revenue drops to EBITDA.

Q: What drove the 35% growth? A: Client numbers grew about 15% a year, premium per client about 12% (mostly medical inflation and group health repricing), and the take rate rose from 11% to 13% of premium placed over three years.
Q: How sticky are clients? A: About 88% renew each year, down from 93% three years ago.
Q: What does the fund need? A: A five-year hold, exit by IPO or sale, and a 3x money multiple; there is no debt in the structure.

modelTree.label: Should the fund buy 60% at ₹2,000 crore (25x EBITDA) and make 3x?

children.label: Market: SME group health and property cover
Average premium per SME (medical inflation, repricing)
Share placed by brokers vs agents and insurers' direct sales
Insurer rewards and marketing fees (about 40%, under scrutiny)
Insurer concentration (top three give 55% of revenue)
New client wins (sales headcount, new cities)
Premium per client compared with the market
Take rate (11% to 13% of premium placed)
Downside: 20% a year to about ₹200 crore
Base: 30% a year to about ₹300 crore
Upside: 35% a year to about ₹360 crore
Sale to a larger broker or financial group

hypotheses: Only about 15 points of the 35% growth is volume the broker controls; the rest is medical inflation and higher reward rates, neither of which is likely to repeat at the same pace.

Insurer rewards (about ₹128 crore of revenue) are exposed as group health insurers run claims ratios above 90% and regulators scrutinise payouts to intermediaries. Halving them removes about ₹64 crore; if, as is likely for pure insurer fees, almost no cost falls away with that revenue, EBITDA drops from about ₹80 crore to about ₹16 crore (down 80%), and even if a third of the lost revenue were offset by lower sales incentives, EBITDA would still fall by about half.
At 20% growth and a 20x exit multiple the fund makes about 2x, not 3x, so the price only works if 30% growth holds.
hints: Work backwards from the return: what must be true about the business today and tomorrow for the fund to make 3x?
Four branches: market, quality of today's EBITDA, can revenue grow 30% a year, returns and exit.
Market splits into growth of the SME premium pool (more SMEs buying cover, premium per SME) and the share placed by brokers.

keyMetrics.name: Revenue growth decomposition
keyMetrics.formula: (1 + client growth) x (1 + premium per client growth) x (1 + take rate change) - 1 ≈ 1.15 x 1.12 x 1.06 - 1 ≈ 36%

keyMetrics.name: Money multiple
keyMetrics.formula: (exit EBITDA x exit multiple x 60%) / ₹1,200 crore invested

keyMetrics.name: Take rate
keyMetrics.formula: broker revenue / premium placed

commonMistakes: Extrapolating 35% growth without separating volume (clients) from price (medical inflation) and take rate.
Valuing all revenue at the same multiple when 40% depends on discretionary insurer rewards exposed to regulation and to insurers' own losses.

frameworkPick.why: A financial investor deciding whether to buy needs diligence on market, earnings quality, returns and exit; the deal stands or falls on whether 30% growth is real, so a growth decomposition is the second lens.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Margins are a healthy 25%; the question is whether the price is backed by durable earnings and growth, which a margin diagnosis alone cannot answer.
distractorWhyNot.ma: A strategic M&A lens centres on fit and synergies with the buyer's business, which a financial investor does not have here.

tree.label: Why has a general insurer's profit before tax fallen?

flaws.explanation: The tree covers only the underwriting result. Insurers also earn investment income on the float (premiums held before claims are paid), which is often what makes Indian general insurers profitable at all; a fall in yields or a smaller float can cut profit with no change in underwriting.
flaws.fix: Add a fourth branch, 'Investment income on the float', split into size of the investment book and investment yield.

correctedTree.label: Why has a general insurer's profit before tax fallen?

tree.label: Annual retail term insurance premium in India

Average sum assured paid per claim

flaws.explanation: Market size here is policyholders x average annual premium. Death claims are what insurers pay out, not what customers pay in; they matter for insurer profitability, but they are not a component of the premium pool.
flaws.fix: Remove the claims branch; premium pool = number of term policyholders x average annual premium.

Looks out of place in a list of customer reasons, but involuntary lapses (no mandate, failed debit) are a real and separate cause, often the cheapest to fix.

tree.label: How can a standalone health insurer grow retail premium 20% a year?

Stop customers porting to rival insurers
Stop customers moving to employer group cover
Customers buy more cover (higher sum insured, add-ons, more members)
Higher premium for the same cover (rate revisions, age-band step-ups)

flaws.explanation: Customers who leave at renewal either port to a rival, move to group cover, or simply stop having health cover at all. The last group, often driven by price or forgetfulness, is missing, and it is usually a large share of non-renewals.
flaws.fix: Add 'Stop customers dropping cover altogether (price, affordability, forgetting)'.

Stop customers porting to rival insurers
Stop customers moving to employer group cover
Stop customers dropping cover altogether (price, affordability, forgetting)
Customers buy more cover (higher sum insured, add-ons, more members)
Higher premium for the same cover (rate revisions, age-band step-ups)

decoys.whyFine: Looks like filler, but insurance marketing firms and common service centres are real IRDAI-recognised channels, so the channel list stays complete.
Looks outside the insurer's control, but losing retail customers to employer cover is a real, measurable source of non-renewal.

flaws.title: Rising health claims cost per life

tree.label: Why has retail health claims cost per insured life risen 14% in a year?

Share with pre-existing conditions now past the waiting period
Admission rate for the same profile

Shift to costlier non-network or premium hospitals
Higher package rates for common surgeries
Procedures, tests and consumables per admission

flaws.explanation: Claims cost per life is claim frequency x average cost per claim. Premium adequacy is about what the insurer charges, not what it pays out; it matters for the claims ratio, but it does not drive claims cost.
flaws.fix: Remove the premium branch. If the real question is the claims ratio, change the root and add premium as the denominator.

flaws.explanation: Package rates for surgeries are part of network hospital tariffs, so 'higher package rates' is the same increase as 'network hospital tariff increases' in different words and would double-count it.
flaws.fix: Remove it; tariff increases already cover package rates.

Admission rate for the same profile
Price per service (tariffs and hospital mix)
Shift to costlier non-network or premium hospitals
Procedures, tests and consumables per admission

decoys.whyFine: Looks like a one-off detail, but as waiting periods expire, pre-existing conditions become claimable, which genuinely raises claim frequency.
Looks like an overlap with tariff increases, but it is a change in hospital mix at constant tariffs, a separate price driver.

flaws.title: Life insurer's falling value of new business

children.label: Fewer term plans and more ULIPs being sold
Premium rates and charges relative to benefits
Investment returns and discount rates (economic assumptions)

flaws.explanation: A shift from term to ULIPs is a change in product mix, which the 'Product mix of APE' branch already covers. Placing it under volume, in different words, double-counts the most likely cause of the VNB fall (term carries far higher margins than ULIPs).
flaws.fix: Remove it from the APE branch; the mix branch captures it through the term and ULIP shares.

flaws.explanation: VNB margin is the present value of future profits on new policies, so it depends heavily on how long customers are assumed to keep paying. Persistency (lapse) assumptions are missing, yet when lapse experience worsens and assumptions are revised, a few points of persistency can cut margins sharply because upfront acquisition costs are recovered only from later premiums.
flaws.fix: Add 'Persistency (share of policies still paying in later years)' alongside the other margin assumptions.

Persistency (share of policies still paying in later years)
Investment returns and discount rates (economic assumptions)

decoys.whyFine: Looks like a balance-sheet item rather than a margin driver, but the cost of holding required capital is deducted in calculating VNB.
Looks irrelevant because APE is flat, but flat APE can hide offsetting channel moves; it belongs in the tree and the data will rule it out.

flaws.fix: Move it under Medical tests as a general node, 'Repeat tests after failed or abnormal samples'.

chainDrills.prompt: A new retail health product's claims ratio is far above plan in its first year, driven by maternity claims. The product was designed with a nine-month waiting period for maternity, much shorter than most rival products, and underwriting followed its guidelines. Where does the root cause sit?
chainDrills.why: The cost appears in claims, and underwriting looks like a suspect, but underwriters applied the guidelines correctly. The short waiting period is a product design choice that invites people planning a pregnancy to buy, so the root cause is in Product design and pricing.

chainDrills.prompt: Put the stages of the standard insurance value chain in order, from designing a product to managing the money and risk it generates.
chainDrills.why: A product is designed and priced, sold by a distributor, underwritten and issued, then serviced and renewed while claims are handled; investments, reinsurance and capital management sit at the end because they manage the float and risk that all earlier stages create.

chainDrills.prompt: A motor insurer's own-damage claims within 30 days of policy start jump fivefold on 'break-in' policies (renewals after the old policy lapsed), most of them sourced by one broker. Last year the insurer replaced surveyor pre-inspections for these cases with customer-uploaded photos that are not checked. Where does the root cause sit?
chainDrills.why: The losses appear in claims and cluster at one broker, but the broker is only where the cases come from. Accepting pre-existing damage because the inspection check was removed is a risk-selection failure, so the root cause is in Underwriting and issuance.

chainDrills.prompt: Assign each item to the stage where it arises.

items.item: Salvage recovered on a written-off car
Actuarial work to file a new health product with IRDAI
Renewal commission paid to the agent who sold the policy
Pre-issuance medical tests for a term proposal
Premium ceded under a quota-share reinsurance treaty
Lead fee paid to a web aggregator

chainDrills.why: Renewal commission feels like distribution, but it is paid to keep an existing policy in force and sits with renewals and servicing. Medical tests feel like a health cost, but they are part of deciding whether to accept the risk. Salvage is a recovery that reduces the net cost of a claim, so it belongs to claims. Reinsurance premium is a risk-transfer and capital decision, not a claims cost.

chainDrills.prompt: A general insurer's profit before tax falls by a third even though its combined ratio is unchanged at 104%. Which stage most likely explains it?
chainDrills.why: An unchanged combined ratio means premium, claims, commission and expenses moved together, so underwriting did not change. The fall must come from investment income on the float, for example lower yields or smaller realised gains, which sits in Investments, reinsurance and capital.

chainDrills.prompt: A life insurer's VNB margin falls because more policies lapse after year one than assumed. The lapses are concentrated in policies sold by one bank partner that was recently offered much higher first-year commission. Renewal premiums for all channels are collected through the insurer's own reminder and auto-debit process, which works equally well across channels, and lapsed customers often say they were not told the premium was due every year. Where does the root cause sit?
chainDrills.why: Lapses show up in Policy servicing and renewals, but servicing is the same for every channel and performs equally well. The pattern (one partner, a recent jump in first-year commission, customers unaware of a recurring premium) points to sales incentives encouraging unsuitable or pushed sales, so the root cause is in Distribution and sales.
